title: Walk down into the Roman Forum
description: The political heart of the empire for a thousand years, now a jumble of broken columns most people rush through on the way to the Colosseum. The combined ticket includes Palatine Hill - budget half a day for both, not twenty minutes.

title: Look down on the Forum from Palatine Hill
description: Where Rome was supposedly founded, and where emperors later built palaces so vast the word palace comes from this hill's name. Far fewer visitors climb up here than stay down among the Forum's ruins.

title: Throw a coin backward into the Trevi Fountain
description: Around 3,000 euros a day gets fished out and given to a Catholic charity for the poor. Come before 7am if you want a photo without a hundred other raised phones in it.

title: Sit on the Spanish Steps at Piazza di Spagna
description: Actually paid for by a French diplomat, not the Spanish, who only lent their name via the embassy at the bottom. Sitting on the steps to eat is now fined, and the ban is enforced.

title: See the she-wolf at the Capitoline Museums
description: The oldest public museum in the world, opened in 1471, on the hill Rome's civic government still runs from. The underground passage between the two palazzos has the best view of the Forum you'll get for free.

title: Walk the empty streets of Ostia Antica
description: Rome's former port city, as complete as Pompeii but a 40-minute train ride from the centre instead of a day trip, and with a fraction of the visitors.

title: Watch the Palio horse race in Siena
description: Ten horses, bareback, three laps of the Piazza del Campo packed with tens of thousands of people - run on 2 July and 16 August by rival city districts that take it more seriously than any national sport.

title: Climb the Arc de Triomphe for the view down the Champs-Elysees
description: 284 steps to the terrace, and the only place you can actually see the twelve avenues radiating from the Etoile - from the ground it just looks like a very busy roundabout.

title: Stand inside the stained glass of Sainte-Chapelle
description: Fifteen soaring windows telling the entire Bible in over a thousand painted-glass panels, built in under six years to house a single relic. Go on a bright morning - the whole effect depends on the sun.

title: Walk the Hall of Mirrors at the Chateau de Versailles
description: 357 mirrors facing seventeen garden windows, built to outshine Louis XIV's rivals and later the room where the treaty ending the First World War was signed. Book a timed palace ticket separately from the gardens.

title: Stand among the graves at the Normandy American Cemetery
description: 9,388 white crosses and Stars of David above Omaha Beach, precisely aligned so they line up from any angle. Pointe du Hoc, the cliff the Rangers scaled under fire, is a short drive further along the coast and still cratered from the naval bombardment.

title: See the Crown Jewels at the Tower of London
description: The jewels sit on a moving walkway to keep the queue flowing, so loop back around for a second pass if you want longer than the ten seconds you get the first time. The ravens are famously never allowed to leave.

title: Walk the tombs of Westminster Abbey
description: Seventeen monarchs are buried here alongside Darwin, Newton and Dickens, packed so densely you are often standing on someone's grave marker without realising. Closed to sightseers on Sundays for services.

title: Walk the terrace above the Roman Baths
description: The Great Bath still holds the original Roman lead lining and green, algae-lit water you cannot enter - for the actual swim, cross the street to the rooftop pool at Thermae instead.

title: See the Honours of Scotland at Edinburgh Castle
description: Built on an extinct volcanic plug fortified for 3,000 years - the one o'clock gun still fires daily, a habit that started so ships in the Forth could set their clocks.

title: Get lost in the gardens of the Real Alcazar
description: A working royal palace since the 14th century, still used by the Spanish royal family, with Mudejar work so fine it's often mistaken for Granada's Alhambra. Its gardens doubled as the Water Gardens of Dorne in Game of Thrones.

title: See the Botafumeiro swing at Santiago Cathedral
description: The endpoint of the Camino, where exhausted pilgrims arrive to a giant censer swung on ropes across the transept, trailing incense smoke - it only flies at specific masses, so check the schedule before you plan around it.

title: Stand under the Brandenburg Gate
description: Built as a Prussian city gate, later stranded in the death strip between East and West Berlin for 28 years - the Quadriga on top faces east, having been carried off by Napoleon and brought back facing the other way.

title: Walk the grounds of the Dachau concentration camp memorial
description: The first Nazi concentration camp, opened in 1933 as a model for the rest of the system, a 20-minute train from central Munich. Free entry, and the audio guide is worth the small charge - go early, it is a heavier half-day than most people expect.

title: Climb the Torre de Belem
description: Built to guard the mouth of the Tagus just as Portugal's Age of Discovery ships were sailing out of it - a UNESCO site with a queue that moves slowly through one narrow spiral staircase, so go at opening.

title: See the tomb of Vasco da Gama at the Jeronimos Monastery
description: Funded by a tax on the spice trade the explorers it commemorates opened up - the cloister alone justifies the ticket, and it sits a five-minute walk from the original pasteis de nata bakery.

title: See the painted towers of the Palacio da Pena
description: A 19th-century romantic fantasy in yellow, red and purple, built on the ruins of a monastery struck by lightning - buy a timed park-and-palace ticket online or lose an hour of your day to the queue at the gate.

title: Take the ferry to the Statue of Liberty
description: Crown access is capped at a few hundred people a day and books out weeks ahead - without it you still get Liberty Island and the pedestal, which most visitors don't realise is a separate, easier ticket.

title: Watch the sunset from the Empire State Building
description: The 86th floor observation deck is open-air and the one everyone photographs; the 102nd floor is glassed in and half the size but far less crowded, and both are on the same ticket.

title: Stand in the middle of Times Square after dark
description: Once Manhattan's most notorious red-light district, now lit brighter at midnight than most places at noon - the red TKTS steps above the discount ticket booth are the free seat everyone forgets exists.

title: Tour the White House
description: Free, but you must apply weeks in advance through your member of Congress - without a booked tour, the best you get is the view through the fence from Pennsylvania Avenue or the Ellipse.

title: Hike to the Hollywood Sign viewpoint
description: There is no trail to the letters themselves - the closest legal approach is Griffith Observatory or the Mount Lee gate, both a genuine uphill walk rather than the roadside photo op most tourists expect.

title: Walk Central Park from the reservoir to Bethesda Terrace
description: 843 acres built entirely by hand in the 1850s on swampland and rock, not preserved wilderness - Bow Bridge and Bethesda Terrace are the two spots everyone photographs, and both are busiest at exactly the same golden hour.

title: Watch the Changing of the Guard on Parliament Hill
description: The ceremony only runs in summer and the Peace Tower's Centre Block has been under renovation for years - check which parts are actually open before you build a visit around them.

title: See the pilgrims arrive at the Basilica de Guadalupe
description: The most visited Catholic shrine on earth after the Vatican, built where the Virgin is said to have appeared in 1531 - a moving walkway carries the crowds past the original cloak inside the new basilica so nobody lingers too long.

title: Tour Chapultepec Castle
description: The only royal castle in the Americas that actually housed a monarch, briefly, before Mexico's only emperor was overthrown and shot - the view over the city from the terrace explains why every regime since has wanted the hill.

title: Walk the ramparts of the Red Fort
description: Mughal red sandstone walls over two kilometres around, where India's prime minister still raises the flag every Independence Day - go early, since the site closes by late afternoon and Mondays are shut entirely.

title: Watch the ferries leave from the Gateway of India
description: Built for a royal visit that had already happened by the time it was finished, and later the exit point for the last British troops leaving India in 1948 - the boat to Elephanta Island leaves from the jetty right beside it.

title: Look through the 953 windows of the Hawa Mahal
description: Built so royal women could watch street life below without being seen themselves - the honeycomb facade looks solid from the street, but from inside almost every panel is a window.

title: Stand on the wooden stage at Kiyomizu-dera
description: Built without a single nail, on a hillside stage 13m up that gave rise to a Japanese idiom for taking a leap of faith. Come at dawn or after the tour buses for a version of the view without the crowd in it.

title: Climb Osaka Castle for the skyline view
description: Rebuilt in concrete in the 1930s after the original burned during a 16th-century siege, and now with a lift to the top - the moat's cherry blossoms in spring draw as many people as the castle itself.
